# How much resin do I need?

> Calculate rectangular or cylindrical mold volume, subtract displaced volume and add a chosen allowance. Optional component volumes apply only when the manufacturer specifies a ratio by volume.

## Calculator
- [Open the calculator](https://metricotter.com/): A 10 × 5 × 2 cm rectangular mold with no displacement and 10% extra needs 110 mL of mixed product.

## Guide
- [How to work out how much resin you need](https://metricotter.com/guide/): step-by-step measuring, common mistakes, formula, limits and a worked example.

## Method
Rectangular volume is length × width × depth; cylindrical volume is π × (diameter ÷ 2)² × depth. A cubic centimetre is one millilitre. Subtract displaced volume per mold, multiply by mold count, then add the allowance. For a stated volume ratio A:B, split the total in those proportions.

## Limits
The example 2:1 ratio is illustrative. Enter the exact ratio and measurement basis from your product instructions. Do not use the component-volume results for a ratio specified by mass. Do not guess density to convert a mass ratio. Follow the manufacturer’s mixing, batch-size and handling instructions.

## Supporting pages
- [Method and assumptions](https://metricotter.com/method/)
- [About, editorial responsibility and privacy](https://metricotter.com/about/)

## Sources
- [NIST: SI units and measurement](https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/metric-si/si-units)

## Step by step
1. Measure the inside of the mold: length and width for a rectangle, or the diameter for a round mold, plus the depth you will fill.
2. Work out the volume. For a rectangle multiply length × width × depth; for a cylinder use π × radius² × depth. One cubic centimetre is one millilitre.
3. Subtract the volume of anything you embed, such as wood, stones or dried flowers.
4. Add an allowance for resin left in the cup, then split the total into parts A and B using the ratio on the product.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing by weight when the product gives a volume ratio, or the other way round. The two ratios are usually different.
- Pouring deeper than the product's maximum layer thickness. Deep pours can overheat and crack.
- Mixing too little and having to make a second batch in the middle of a pour.

## Worked examples
### Example 1
A 10 × 5 × 2 cm rectangular mold with no displacement and 10% extra needs 110 mL of mixed product.

### Example 2
A cylinder 10 cm in diameter and 2 cm deep holds about 157.08 mL before any allowance.

### Example 3
Only if the product specifies 2:1 by volume, a 110 mL batch splits into about 73.33 mL A and 36.67 mL B.
